description: Phillip Jones, a retired Air Force colonel, recalls serving as deputy A5 at U.S. CENTAF at Shaw Air Force Base on September 11, 2001. He describes watching the second airplane strike on television and realizing the event was not an accident. Jones sent staff and conference attendees home, then helped cancel programs, arrange support for personnel in Egypt, and prepare orders to deploy forces to the Middle East. He recalls that the UAE visitors were in Sumter, South Carolina, where they had been roughed up and confined to their rooms, while the Egyptian personnel remained in Egypt. Jones says he worked for about 90 days without a day off, coordinating transportation for forces and units deploying to the Middle East, and later helped plan for Afghanistan and the Iraq war. He also remembers his friend Dwayne Williams, an Army major who perished, and reflects on the loss to Williams’s family and friends.

entities_and_facets.perspective: First-person recollection by a military planner of watching television coverage and responding from Shaw Air Force Base; the account does not describe his presence at an attack site.

planning war in the Middle East, we might be a target as well. I made everybody go home. And of course, we didn't have a plan at that point on what to do next, but we knew that we had to. description_support.text: He recalls that the UAE visitors were in Sumter, South Carolina, where they had been roughed up and confined to their rooms, while the Egyptian personnel remained in Egypt.

support.quote: ourselves, Hey, I wonder what happened to those guys from the UAE that we sent back home to the hotel in Sumter, South Carolina. So we went to check on them, and they were locked in their rooms because they'd been roughed up pretty good by the local population. So they hadn't eaten in three days other than what they could get out of a vending machine. So we brought them onto the base, put them on the quarters, and then we didn't know how we were going to get them or the Egyptians back because they were not going to be in airplanes flying out. And even if they were, nobody was going to be getting on an airplane with a bunch of Arabs flying back to the Middle East. So we had to get military transport to come in and get those guys home. But from that point on, for about the next 90 days, I didn't have a day off. And the A-5, the actual A-5 deployed to the Middle East to run the air

operations center, and I was responsible back home to make sure that we worked all of the transportation for all the forces and all the units that were deploying to the Middle East. It wasn't until about Thanksgiving that I got a day off. And, you know, those things continued on for however many years. You know the history: Afghanistan, then the war in Iraq. And I was very instrumental in planning that as well. And we worked our butts off trying to make sure that the people had what they needed, where they needed it, in time to get it there. In the meantime, the poor guys that were stuck in Egypt, they had to make do with what they did. And the major that was in charge from my office did an outstanding job of protecting the people, figuring out how to get some money so he could pay to have the support that he needed, because the support wasn't coming. That was not a priority anymore.
